title: Bagmati Corridor Flood Simulation with Hami Nepal
description: An exploratory drone mapping, HEC-RAS 2D modelling, and GIS exposure study from Sundarijal to Dhobighat, combining corridor-scale simulation with detailed orthomosaics in selected vulnerable areas.
dataPointsRaw:
Modelled reach: Approx. 27–30 km
Makalbari exposure: Approx. 1,541 buildings
Tinkune–Dhobighat exposure: Approx. 1,770 buildings
Scenario input: Demo discharge data
fullText:
In June 2026, I handled the Bagmati Corridor drone mapping and flood-simulation workflow through Airlift Technology in collaboration with Hami Nepal. I worked across project coordination, drone piloting, imagery processing, hydraulic modelling, and GIS-based exposure analysis.

The study modelled the river corridor from Sundarijal to Dhobighat, while drone surveys focused on selected historically flood-prone locations. The results describe an exploratory scenario based on demo discharge inputs prepared from rainfall-trend interpretation. Calibration with observed flows remains a next step.

## My role across the full workflow

I handled the work from field mapping to the final spatial outputs. This connected the aerial surveys, terrain preparation, simulation, and interpretation within one workflow.

- **Project coordination:** organised the work across the mapping, modelling, and analysis stages.
- **Drone piloting:** surveyed selected vulnerable sections of the corridor.
- **Imagery processing:** generated detailed orthomosaics for local interpretation.
- **Hydraulic modelling:** prepared the terrain and configured the HEC-RAS 2D simulation.
- **GIS analysis:** refined the simulated flood boundary and overlaid building footprints.
- **Output preparation:** brought the scenario maps and simulation video together for review.
- **Presentation and training:** presented the work to the APF disaster rescue team and trained them to use maps and 3D models.

## A corridor-scale model with local detail

The model covered approximately 27–30 km of the Bagmati River between Sundarijal and Dhobighat. A satellite-based DEM supplied the main terrain surface for this reach.

Drone mapping covered selected vulnerable locations, including Makalbari and the Tinkune–Dhobighat section. These orthomosaics made it possible to interpret the simulated boundary against visible buildings, roads, riverbanks, and open areas at a finer local scale.

### Two complementary scales

- **Corridor view:** model the connected river reach using the available elevation dataset.
- **Local view:** use drone imagery to examine selected vulnerable areas in detail.

## From rainfall assumptions to flood maps

I prepared representative discharge inputs from rainfall-trend interpretation and hydrological assumptions because continuous, high-resolution discharge records were limited.

In HEC-RAS, the setup used a 2D computational mesh, an upstream inflow hydrograph, and a downstream normal-depth condition. The unsteady-flow simulation produced water-depth, velocity, and inundation outputs.

1. **Prepare terrain:** clip and preprocess the satellite DEM for the study reach.
2. **Configure the model:** define the flow area, computational mesh, and boundary conditions.
3. **Run the scenario:** generate simulated depth, velocity, and flood extent.
4. **Refine in GIS:** convert the depth raster into a flood-boundary polygon and improve its interpretability.
5. **Assess exposure:** overlay the boundary with orthomosaics and building footprints.
6. **Communicate the outputs:** prepare maps and a simulation walkthrough.

## The simulated corridor extent

The corridor map shows the scenario's inundation boundary across the Sundarijal–Dhobighat reach. It provides the broader spatial context for the more detailed local assessments.

The boundary represents the modelled scenario under the chosen input assumptions.

![Scenario-based flood extent along the Bagmati Corridor from Sundarijal to Dhobighat.](/images/bagmati-flood-simulation/corridor-flood-extent.webp)

## Makalbari: interpreting building exposure

At Makalbari, I overlaid the simulated boundary on drone-derived orthomosaic imagery and digitised building footprints. Spatial selection identified approximately 1,541 buildings intersecting the scenario's inundation area.

The count represents potentially exposed structures under the model assumptions.

- **Local evidence:** detailed aerial imagery and mapped building footprints.
- **Analysis:** spatial intersection with the simulated flood boundary.
- **Scenario result:** approximately 1,541 intersecting buildings.
- **Planning use:** a location-specific starting point for further preparedness and exposure review.

![Makalbari scenario map comparing the flood boundary, local imagery, and buildings within the simulated extent.](/images/bagmati-flood-simulation/makalbari-exposure.webp)

## Tinkune to Dhobighat: the urban section

The same overlay approach identified approximately 1,770 buildings intersecting the simulated inundation area in the Tinkune–Dhobighat section.

Combining the modelled boundary with local imagery made the result easier to relate to the developed corridor. It showed where a scenario crossed mapped structures and infrastructure, rather than leaving the result as a standalone hydraulic raster.

![Tinkune to Dhobighat map showing local imagery and the simulated flood-extent boundary.](/images/bagmati-flood-simulation/tinkune-dhobighat-exposure.webp)

## What the outputs contribute

The project brought together a corridor-scale hydraulic scenario and local drone-based interpretation. Its value is in making the relationship between flood assumptions, terrain, and mapped development visible for discussion.

- **Depth and velocity:** spatial outputs showing how the simulated water behaves within the model.
- **Inundation boundary:** a GIS layer that can be compared with other mapped features.
- **Building exposure:** scenario-based counts for the two selected sections.
- **Map and video outputs:** complementary ways to inspect the results.

## Sharing the work with the APF rescue team

I presented the project to the Armed Police Force (APF) disaster rescue team and trained them on using maps and 3D models. This extended my role beyond preparing the spatial outputs to helping the team understand and use them.

- **Presentation:** explain the project and its mapping outputs to the APF disaster rescue team.
- **Practical training:** guide the team in using maps and 3D models.

## Limits and next steps

The simulation used demo discharge data, and the terrain relied primarily on a satellite DEM. Drone imagery was available only for selected locations; it did not cover the entire modelled reach. Boundary assumptions, DEM resolution, and manual refinement of the flood polygon also influence the outputs.

Further work would need observed discharge records, calibration and validation, improved terrain, and additional drone coverage. Future collaboration with DHM and relevant authorities could strengthen the input data and practical use of the work.
